incidents.title: United States: Espionage Act conviction of Samuel Loring Morison for leaking satellite photographs to Jane's Defence Weekly, 1985 to 1988
incidents.summary: Naval intelligence analyst Samuel Loring Morison was convicted under the Espionage Act after he sent classified satellite photographs to a British defense publication in 1984. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit upheld his conviction in 1988, rejecting his argument that giving the images to the press was protected by the First Amendment.
incidents.what_happened: Samuel Loring Morison worked as an intelligence analyst at the Naval Intelligence Support Center in Suitland, Maryland, where he had access to classified material and had signed a nondisclosure agreement as a condition of his employment. In 1984 he sent two classified KH-11 satellite photographs showing construction of a Soviet Kiev-class aircraft carrier to Jane's Defence Weekly, a British publication on military affairs, which published them. Federal prosecutors charged Morison under two sections of the Espionage Act of 1917, one covering disclosure of national defense information to a foreign government and one covering disclosure to any other recipient, including a news organization, along with a separate federal charge of theft of government property. A jury convicted him on all counts. On appeal, Morison argued that applying the Espionage Act to a disclosure made to a news organization violated the First Amendment. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, the federal appeals court based in Richmond, Virginia, rejected that argument. Writing for the court, Judge Donald Stewart Russell held that the Espionage Act's disclosure provisions applied to the press as well as to foreign governments, and the court affirmed the conviction in 1988. The Supreme Court of the United States declined to review the case.
incidents.stated_justification: The Fourth Circuit said the Espionage Act's disclosure provisions were not limited to transmissions to foreign governments, and it separately described the related federal law Morison was also convicted under as "a criminal statute covering the theft of government property."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Citing Branzburg v. Hayes, a 1972 Supreme Court decision, the Fourth Circuit said journalists had no special protection simply because they were transmitting information to the media, leaving the source of a leak, rather than the publication that printed it, open to an Espionage Act prosecution.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The case tested whether the Espionage Act of 1917, written to penalize wartime aid to a foreign enemy, could also be used against someone who gave classified material to a widely read defense publication rather than to an opposing government.
incidents.outcome_note: President Bill Clinton pardoned Morison, according to the First Amendment Encyclopedia, though no court reversed the Fourth Circuit's decision upholding his conviction.

incidents.title: United States: Pentagon press pool kept from the opening hours of the Panama invasion, December 1989
incidents.summary: When United States forces invaded Panama on December 20, 1989, the Pentagon kept its national media pool of reporters away from the opening hours of the fighting. President George H.W. Bush later told newspaper editors the arrangement had again failed to get journalists to the action.
incidents.what_happened: United States forces invaded Panama on December 20, 1989, in an operation aimed at removing General Manuel Noriega from power. The Department of Defense activated its national media pool, a standing rotation of reporters created in April 1985 after journalists were excluded from the 1983 invasion of Grenada, but the Pentagon kept the pool away from the fighting for its opening hours. NBC News correspondent Fred Francis watched the early combat from a golf course three miles from the action rather than from the battlefield itself. Pooled reporters who reached Panama grew frustrated when Pentagon briefings described the fighting as over while Panamanians were still reporting gunfire by telephone, and journalist Peter Arnett later said the civilian death toll around Noriega's headquarters was never confirmed by the United States government. At an April 6, 1990 meeting with newspaper editors, a questioner told President George H.W. Bush that the Panama pool had again shown the arrangement for covering the opening of a military operation was not working. Bush said reporters who felt they had been denied access should be given it once they arrived.
incidents.stated_justification: President Bush told the editors that constraints on press access were part of any combat situation, saying, "When you're involved in a combat situation, I don't need to tell people in this room there are constraints."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: NBC's Fred Francis watched the invasion's opening hours from a golf course three miles from the fighting, and journalist Peter Arnett later said the civilian toll around Noriega's headquarters was never acknowledged by the United States government.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Panama pool was the first major test of the national media pool system the Pentagon created in April 1985 after journalists had been kept off the island during the 1983 invasion of Grenada.
incidents.outcome_note: President Bush told newspaper editors on April 6, 1990, that journalists who felt they had been denied access during the Panama pool should be given it once they arrived in the future.

incidents.title: Soviet Union: arrest and seven-week detention of American correspondent Nicholas Daniloff in Moscow, 1986
incidents.summary: Soviet authorities arrested Nicholas Daniloff, the Moscow correspondent for U.S. News & World Report, on August 30, 1986, days after the United States arrested a Soviet United Nations employee on espionage charges. Daniloff was held for two weeks before being moved to United States Embassy custody and left the Soviet Union on September 29, 1986.
incidents.what_happened: Nicholas Daniloff, the Moscow correspondent for the magazine U.S. News & World Report, was arrested by Soviet authorities on August 30, 1986, days after the United States arrested Gennadi Zakharov, a Soviet employee of the United Nations, on espionage charges in New York. President Ronald Reagan told the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 1986, that an American correspondent in Moscow had been made the subject of what he called fabricated accusations and trumped-up charges, arrested and jailed in disregard of due process, and in effect held as a hostage. The White House said Secretary of State George Shultz would raise Daniloff's case as the first item at his meeting that week with Soviet Foreign Minister Eduard Shevardnadze. On September 12, 1986, Daniloff was transferred from Soviet custody to the United States Ambassador in Moscow, ending confinement Reagan described as an 8-by-10-foot cell shared with a suspected informant and daily interrogation. Daniloff left the Soviet Union for the West on September 29, 1986. The Committee to Protect Journalists later named his case among "meritless espionage cases brought against journalists."
incidents.stated_justification: Soviet officials' own account of the espionage accusation does not appear among the sources reviewed here; President Reagan told the United Nations General Assembly that Daniloff had been made the subject of "fabricated accusations and trumped-up charges."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Daniloff was held, in Reagan's description, in an 8-by-10-foot cell shared with a suspected informant and subjected to hours of interrogation before he was transferred to United States Ambassador custody on September 12, 1986.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Daniloff's arrest came days after the United States arrested Gennadi Zakharov, a Soviet employee at the United Nations, on espionage charges in New York, and the two cases became linked in the following weeks of diplomacy.
incidents.outcome_note: Daniloff left Moscow for the West on September 29, 1986, though the White House denied that his departure and Zakharov's release amounted to a formal exchange.

incidents.title: Malaysia: Printing Presses and Publications Act amended to bar court review of publishing permits, 1987
incidents.summary: Malaysia's government amended the Printing Presses and Publications Act in 1987 to expand its power to ban or restrict publications and to bar any court challenge to the suspension or revocation of a publishing permit. The change came the same year Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's government arrested 106 opposition politicians and activists in an operation known by the codename Lalang.
incidents.what_happened: Malaysia's Printing Presses and Publications Act of 1984 already required every newspaper and periodical to hold an annual publishing permit issued by the government. In 1987 the government of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad amended the act to make the publication of what it called malicious news a punishable offense, to expand the government's power to ban or restrict publications, and to prohibit any court challenge to the suspension or revocation of a publishing permit. The amendment came the same year Mahathir's government carried out a wide arrest operation known by the codename Lalang, a Malay word for a weed. In October 1987 Mahathir ordered the arrest of 106 people, including politicians from the opposition Democratic Action Party and Parti Islam Se Malaysia, along with human rights activists, under the Internal Security Act, which allows detention without trial. Malaysia's courts had shown some willingness to review the legality of the government's actions, but Mahathir responded by removing five high court judges and introducing a provision barring judicial review of security detentions.
incidents.stated_justification: Malaysian officials did not state, in the sources reviewed here, a specific public reason for the 1987 amendment beyond barring the publication of what the law itself called "malicious news."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The United States State Department later said government power over licensing and other policies helped create "an atmosphere that inhibits independent or investigative journalism and results in extensive self-censorship."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The press-law amendment followed Mahathir's use of the Internal Security Act against political opponents and activists in October 1987, at a time when Malaysia's courts had begun reviewing legal challenges to his own conduct in office.
incidents.outcome_note: The 1987 amendments to the Printing Presses and Publications Act remained in force, according to the United States State Department's account of Malaysia's press law.
